title: Opening: old age as absurdity
short: The poem opens with an outburst against old age, felt as a ludicrous thing tied to a still-passionate imagination.
body: Yeats wrote 'The Tower' at Thoor Ballylee, the Norman tower near Gort, Co. Galway, that he had bought in 1917; in the 1928 volume it is dated 1926, and Jeffares places its drafting in 1925, when Yeats turned sixty. Part I sets out the quarrel the whole poem tries to settle: the body is 'decrepit', yet the imagination has never been more 'excited, passionate, fantastical'. The comparison of age to something tied to a dog's tail is deliberately undignified, and it returns at the end of the stanza as 'a sort of battered kettle at the heel', the tin can that boys tie to a dog. The poem as a whole moves from complaint (I), through a summoning of local ghosts to question them (II), to a testament (III).

title: Ben Bulben
short: The flat-topped mountain north of Sligo, the landscape of Yeats's boyhood holidays with his Pollexfen relations.
body: Ben Bulben (Irish Binn Ghulbain) dominates the country around Sligo town, where Yeats spent long childhood summers with his mother's family, the Pollexfens. Recalling himself fishing its streams 'with rod and fly, / Or the humbler worm', he sets the boy's unlimited summer day against the old man's limited time. The mountain was to become Yeats's emblem of home and of the legendary west: his late poem 'Under Ben Bulben' (1938) names it in its title and ends with the instructions for his grave at nearby Drumcliff. The fishing image also prepares the will in Part III, where the heirs are men who climb the streams at dawn and 'drop their cast'.

title: Plato and Plotinus
short: The two philosophers stand for abstract, other-worldly thought, the consolation conventionally offered to the old once the Muse has gone.
body: Plato (c. 427-347 BC) and the Neoplatonist Plotinus (AD 204/5-270) represent the life of argument and 'abstract things' that age seems to impose: both taught that true reality lies beyond the senses, so that the body and its passions are a prison to escape. Yeats had been reading Stephen MacKenna's translation of Plotinus's Enneads (1917-30). Part I accepts this programme only grudgingly ('It seems that I must'), and Part III reverses it: 'I mock Plotinus' thought / And cry in Plato's teeth'. Yeats's own note later admitted that Plotinus himself had said something close to Yeats's position, that soul is the maker of all things.

title: battered kettle at the heel
short: The tin can tied to a dog's tail: old age as an object of derision, rattling after the poet.
body: The image completes the comparison at l. 4, where age is tied to the poet 'as to a dog's tail'. Tying a kettle or tin can to a dog's tail was a common boys' cruelty, and the noise made the dog ridiculous as it ran. Yeats offers two options, both humiliating: either give up imagination for philosophy, or be mocked by the clattering presence of his own decrepitude. The colloquial bathos is typical of the later Yeats, who mixes grand rhetoric with plain and even comic diction; compare the 'tattered coat upon a stick' of 'Sailing to Byzantium', written in the same period.

title: Mrs. French
short: An eighteenth-century lady of Peterswell, near Ballylee, whose servant cut off a farmer's ears to please her.
body: Yeats's note identifies her as a Mrs French who lived at Peterswell in the eighteenth century and was related to Sir Jonah Barrington, the Irish judge and memoirist (1760-1834), who told the story of the ears and the trouble it caused in his Personal Sketches of His Own Times (1827-32). The anecdote shows the old Ascendancy world of candlesticks, mahogany and wine and its casual violence: the servant 'divines' an unspoken wish and acts on it. Yeats tells it with a cool, almost comic precision ('a little covered dish'). When she returns in the roll-call she is 'Gifted with so fine an ear', a grim pun on the clipped ears.

title: the peasant girl (Mary Hynes)
short: Mary Hynes of Ballylee, a famous local beauty, praised in a song by the blind Gaelic poet Raftery.
body: Yeats's note names the beauty and the poet as Mary Hynes and Raftery. Antoine Ó Raifteirí (c. 1779-1835), a blind itinerant poet of Co. Mayo and Galway, made an Irish song in praise of Mary Hynes of Ballylee. Yeats had collected stories of both from old people near Gort in the 1890s and printed them in 'Dust Hath Closed Helen's Eye' in The Celtic Twilight, with local memories of her beauty. The stanza shows how song gives glory: farmers 'jostled at the fair' just to see her. The country girl thus becomes a local Helen, and the next stanzas extend the parallel.

title: the bog of Cloone
short: A man who set out by night to see Mary Hynes, maddened by the song and by drink, fell into Cloone bog and drowned.
body: The story is in The Celtic Twilight ('Dust Hath Closed Helen's Eye'): Yeats records that men drinking and talking of Mary Hynes set out to see her, and that one was drowned in the bog of Cloone. In the poem the men 'mistook the brightness of the moon / For the prosaic light of day'. Moon and sun are a key pair in Yeats: moonlight stands for imagination and subjective vision, daylight for practical, objective fact. The drowned man is the first of the poem's victims of imagination, and his fate sharpens the question of whether poetry's power to 'make men mad' is a triumph or a curse.

title: Homer and Helen
short: The blind Raftery recalls blind Homer, and Mary Hynes recalls Helen, whose beauty caused the Trojan War.
body: Ancient tradition held that Homer was blind (the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, 172, describes its singer as a blind man of Chios). Raftery, also blind, praised a beauty who brought men to ruin; Homer sang of Helen, whose flight with Paris brought Greeks and Trojans to ten years of war. Yeats finds 'nothing strange' in the blind poet's power over sight, because the tragedy of imagination began with Homer. 'Helen has all living hearts betrayed' recalls Yeats's lifelong identification of Maud Gonne with Helen ('No Second Troy', 'The Rose of the World'). In Iliad 3 the Trojan elders, seeing Helen on the walls, admit that men might well suffer for such a woman; Yeats's Celtic Twilight cites the scene in the same connection.

title: 'O may the moon and sunlight seem / One inextricable beam'
short: Yeats prays that imagination (moon) and fact (sun) be fused, since his success as a poet must make men mad.
body: The lines turn the drowned man's mistake into a wish. If the poet triumphs, his songs will be as powerful as Raftery's and so as dangerous; Yeats prays that the moonlight of vision and the sunlight of the prosaic world might become 'one inextricable beam', so that imagination does not lead men astray but becomes their reality. Readers divide on the tone: some hear a proud acceptance of the poet's maddening power, others a troubled awareness of its cost. The sun/moon opposition belongs to the system Yeats was building in A Vision (1925), where solar and lunar stand for objective and subjective natures.

title: Red Hanrahan
short: Yeats's own fictional hero, the wandering Gaelic poet of Stories of Red Hanrahan, who chases a phantom hare and hounds.
body: Owen Hanrahan the Red is a hedge-schoolmaster and poet modelled partly on the eighteenth-century Munster poet Eoghan Rua Ó Súilleabháin. Yeats wrote his stories in the 1890s ('twenty years ago', roughly) for The Secret Rose (1897) and rewrote them with Lady Gregory as Stories of Red Hanrahan (1904). Yeats's note says the chase of the phantom hare and hounds comes from that book: in a barn an old man bewitches a pack of cards, which turn into hounds and a hare, and Hanrahan runs after them and is lost to his love. Including his own invention among real local figures shows that the creatures of imagination are as real to the poet as history.

title: bawn
short: A walled enclosure or cattle-fold attached to an Irish castle or house; here the old barn where the card game was played.
body: The OED derives bawn from Irish bódhún (cow-fort), a fortified enclosure for cattle, and in Irish English it came to mean the yard or outbuilding attached to a house. Yeats uses the Irish word for the barn where, in the Hanrahan story, the 'good fellows shuffled cards'. The rhyme of 'bawn' with 'on' is an approximate one, typical of the half-rhymes in Part II's eight-line stanzas, rhymed aabbcddc. The stanza ends on a dash in mid-sentence ('towards--'), and the next stanza breaks off: Yeats theatrically 'forgets' where Hanrahan was going.

title: the ancient bankrupt master
short: A former owner of Ballylee, ruined by debt, whom no love, music or violence could cheer.
body: Yeats's note says the bankrupt man lived at the castle about a hundred years earlier; one legend held that he could leave only on Sundays, when debtors could not be arrested, and another that he hid in the secret passage. He is the figure of the house itself in decline, so 'harried' that none of the poem's earlier pleasures (love, music, the 'enemy's clipped ear') could please him. 'When he finished his dog's day' picks up the dog of Part I. He returns in the roll-call as the 'old, necessitous, half-mounted man', poor and only half a gentleman.

title: cross-gartered
short: Wearing garters crossed about the leg below and above the knee, an old fashion; the men-at-arms of the tower's Norman owners.
body: Before the bankrupt master, 'for centuries', the tower was a fighting house of the de Burgos, and its men-at-arms climbed the narrow stair either with cross-gartered legs or 'shod in iron'. The word is best known from Twelfth Night, where Malvolio is tricked into appearing 'cross-gartered' in yellow stockings (II.v, III.iv), already an old-fashioned style. Yeats's note adds that the ghosts had been seen playing dice in what was now his bedroom: the 'great wooden dice' beat on the board and break a sleeper's rest.

title: the Great Memory
short: Yeats's term for a universal store of images, the 'Anima Mundi', from which the dead and their images can return.
body: Yeats believed, from his studies in Neoplatonism, theosophy and spiritualism, that individual memories belong to one great memory of nature or of the race. In the essay 'Magic' (1901) he set out the doctrine that 'the borders of our memories are shifting' and that our minds can be evoked by symbols to reveal a single great mind and memory; in Per Amica Silentia Lunae (1918) he called it Anima Mundi, the soul of the world, drawing on Henry More. The ghosts of the men-at-arms are therefore not mere fancies: their images are 'stored' and can come back with 'loud cry and panting breast'.

title: The roll-call of ghosts
short: Yeats summons all the figures of the section at once, each in a riddling epithet, to ask his question.
body: This stanza gathers the cast: the 'half-mounted man' (the bankrupt master), 'beauty's blind rambling celebrant' (Raftery), 'the red man the juggler sent' (Red Hanrahan, sent off by the old conjuror), Mrs French with her 'fine ear', the drowned man, and the 'country wench' (Mary Hynes) whom 'mocking muses' chose for praise. The epithets compress whole stories into a phrase, and the formal summons recalls the Homeric nekuia, Odysseus calling up the dead in Odyssey 11. The question, in the next stanza, is whether all old men and women have raged against age as he does; their eyes, 'impatient to be gone', answer yes, and he dismisses all but Hanrahan.

title: half-mounted
short: Half a gentleman, poorly horsed: a term for the lower, impoverished gentry of eighteenth-century Ireland.
body: Jonah Barrington, the source of the Mrs French story, divided the Irish gentry of his day into three ranks, of which the lowest were the 'half-mounted gentlemen', men of small means who kept up some appearance of gentility. Yeats applies the label to the bankrupt master: 'old, necessitous' (needy) and only half-mounted, a gentleman in decay. The term fits the poem's interest in a social order that is passing, and in Part III Yeats will claim the pride of the Anglo-Irish Protestant tradition at its best.

title: 'Old lecher' and the labyrinth
short: Yeats asks Hanrahan, the experienced lover, whether imagination dwells more on a woman won or a woman lost.
body: Hanrahan, the poet-wanderer with 'a love on every wind', has explored 'the labyrinth of another's being', the maze of erotic intimacy. Yeats asks which haunts the imagination more, the woman won or the woman lost, and answers his own question with self-accusation: if the lost, one must admit having turned aside from the labyrinth out of pride, cowardice, over-subtle thought or 'conscience'. Most critics read this as Yeats's confession about Maud Gonne, whom he courted for decades without success, and perhaps about his hesitations before marriage; memory of that refusal eclipses the sun. The labyrinth, from the Cretan maze of Daedalus, recurs in Yeats as an image of the soul's winding path.

title: The will (Part III)
short: Part III shifts to short three-stress lines and the legal form of a testament: Yeats bequeaths his pride and faith to young men.
body: After the long eight-line stanzas of Part II, Part III runs in brisk lines of three stresses, loosely rhymed, as if the speaker had reached a resolution. The conceit is a legal will. The heirs are 'upstanding men' who fish mountain streams at dawn, recalling the boy on Ben Bulben in Part I: Yeats leaves his inheritance to the active, physical life his 'sedentary trade' has broken in him. The pride he bequeaths is then defined by a series of natural images: the morning, the 'fabulous horn', the sudden shower, the swan's last song.

anchor: people of Burke and of Grattan
title: Burke and Grattan
short: Edmund Burke and Henry Grattan, eighteenth-century Anglo-Irish statesmen, stand for a free, generous Protestant Irish tradition.
body: Edmund Burke (1729-97), political philosopher, and Henry Grattan (1746-1820), leader of the Irish Parliament that won legislative independence in 1782, were heroes of the Anglo-Irish Protestant tradition that Yeats increasingly championed in the 1920s. In his Senate speech on divorce (11 June 1925) he used almost the same phrase: 'We are the people of Burke; we are the people of Grattan'. The pride he describes belongs to people bound 'neither to Cause nor to State', neither to the oppressed nor to oppressors, and who 'gave, though free to refuse': an aristocratic ideal of free generosity. Critics have debated how far this idealises the Ascendancy.

title: the fabulous horn
short: An unexplained legendary horn, perhaps the horn of plenty or a hero's hunting horn; Yeats left no note.
body: Yeats does not say which horn he means, and commentators have not agreed. One reading takes it as the cornucopia, the horn of the goat Amalthea that overflowed with plenty, matching the image of free giving in 'gave, though free to refuse'. Another hears a hero's horn, such as Roland's, or the horn of Fionn and the Fianna in Irish legend, which fits the heroic sense of pride and the sounds of dawn and hunting around it. 'Fabulous' means belonging to fable or legend. Students should note that the image works by sound and suggestion more than by a single reference.

title: the swan's last song
short: The legendary swan-song before death; Yeats noted that he unconsciously echoed T. Sturge Moore's 'Dying Swan'.
body: The belief that swans sing most beautifully just before they die is ancient: in Plato's Phaedo Socrates says swans sing at death not from grief but from joy at going to their god. Yeats makes the dying swan the last image of pride, floating out on a 'glittering stream' to sing. His own note confesses an unconscious debt to 'one of the loveliest lyrics of our time', Thomas Sturge Moore's 'The Dying Swan', which he had often recited on an American lecture tour. Swans are central symbols in Yeats ('The Wild Swans at Coole', 'Leda and the Swan'), and the image points to the poet's own final song.

title: 'I mock Plotinus' thought'
short: Yeats's 'faith': man, not God or the One, made life, death and the universe out of his own soul.
body: Reversing Part I, Yeats rejects the Neoplatonic doctrine that the material world flows down from a higher reality. Instead, 'Death and life were not / Till man made up the whole': the human imagination creates everything, 'sun and moon and star', and even after death 'we rise, / Dream and so create / Translunar Paradise'. His note admits he forgot that Plotinus himself wrote that soul is 'the author of all living things' and 'the maker of the sun' (Enneads V.1.2). The quarrel is therefore more with a popular, transcendental reading of Plato and Plotinus than with Plotinus himself, as several critics observe.

title: Translunar Paradise
short: A paradise beyond the moon, created by the dreaming dead: Yeats's coinage on the old contrast of sublunary and translunary.
body: In ancient and medieval cosmology the region below the moon (sublunary) was the realm of change and decay, and what lay beyond the moon was changeless and divine. 'Translunar' (OED: beyond the moon; also used figuratively of the ethereal) here names the heaven the dead create by dreaming, in keeping with the doctrine of the dreaming-back of souls in A Vision. Michael Drayton had used 'translunary' of Marlowe's imagination ('brave translunary things'), and Yeats's paradise likewise belongs to the imagination. The line completes the faith: man makes not only this world but the next.

title: the daws' nest
short: Jackdaws build in the tower's loophole, the mother bird warming a nest built of twigs heaped layer on layer.
body: Jackdaws (daws) nest in old towers and chimneys. At the arrow-slit or 'loophole' of the tower they pile twig on twig until a mother bird can rest on the 'hollow top' and warm her nest. The image comes in the middle of the will as an emblem of how a tradition is built: by slow accumulation, layer on layer, until it makes a shelter for new life. It also answers the poet's own 'peace', built from 'learned Italian things' and 'the proud stones of Greece'. Compare 'The Stare's Nest by My Window' in 'Meditations in Time of Civil War', where bees build in the loosening masonry of the same tower.

title: 'Now shall I make my soul'
short: To prepare the soul for death by study; the poem ends on the gradual fading of all losses into a bird's sleepy cry.
body: 'To make one's soul' is an old devotional expression, used in Irish and Catholic speech, for preparing oneself for death. Yeats gives it a secular sense: he will compel his soul to study 'in a learned school', recalling the 'singing school' of 'Sailing to Byzantium', until bodily decay, delirium, decrepitude and even the death of friends seem no more than clouds at a fading horizon. The ending modulates from the defiant tone of Part I to quiet acceptance, closing on 'a bird's sleepy cry / Among the deepening shades', where 'shades' means both evening shadows and the ghosts of the dead.
